concepts.title: Remainders and the clock

paragraphs: A clock face only has the numbers 1 to 12. When the hour hand passes 12 it does not go on to 13; it starts again. So the time 17:00 shows as 5 o'clock.
The reason is division with remainder. 17 hours is one full turn of 12 hours plus 5 more: \(17 = 1 \times 12 + 5\). The full turns do not change where the hand points; only the 5 left over does.

We write \(17 \bmod 12 = 5\), read '17 mod 12 is 5'. In general \(a \bmod n\) is the remainder when a is divided by n. It is always one of 0, 1, 2, and so on up to \(n - 1\). On the clock, the top position 12 plays the part of remainder 0.
card.example: Where does the hour hand point 29 hours after midnight? Divide by 12: \(29 = 2 \times 12 + 5\). Two full turns change nothing, so the hand points to 5, and \(29 \bmod 12 = 5\).
card.rule: \(a \bmod n\) is the remainder of a divided by n, a number from 0 to \(n - 1\).
card.limits: It describes whole numbers divided by a positive whole number n. It says nothing about fractions, and the choice of n matters: 17 leaves 5 on a 12-hour clock but 3 on a 7-day week.

media.alt: A clock face whose short hand points at 5 and long hand at 12: 17:00 shown as 5 o'clock.

concepts.title: Congruence: same remainder

paragraphs: Many numbers leave the same remainder: 5, 17 and 29 all leave remainder 5 when divided by 12. On a clock they all point to 5. Mathematicians give this a short name.
We write \(a \equiv b \pmod{n}\), read 'a is congruent to b mod n', when a and b leave the same remainder after division by n. For example \(17 \equiv 5 \pmod{12}\) and \(29 \equiv 17 \pmod{12}\).

There is a second test that needs no remainders. \(a \equiv b \pmod{n}\) exactly when n divides \(a - b\), meaning \(a - b\) is a whole multiple of n. For instance \(29 - 17 = 12\), and 12 is a multiple of 12, so \(29 \equiv 17 \pmod{12}\).
card.example: Is \(40 \equiv 16 \pmod{12}\)? Remainders: \(40 = 3 \times 12 + 4\) and \(16 = 12 + 4\), both 4, so yes. Difference test: \(40 - 16 = 24 = 2 \times 12\), also yes.
card.rule: \(a \equiv b \pmod{n}\) means a and b leave the same remainder when divided by n; equivalently, \(a - b\) is a multiple of n.
card.limits: Congruence is always relative to one chosen n. Two numbers can be congruent mod 12 and not congruent mod 5, so name n every time.

concepts.question: When do two numbers point to the same place on a clock?

questions.q: A clock shows 9 o'clock. What time does it show 5 hours later?
questions.explain: Count on from 9: 10, 11, 12, 1, 2. After 12 the clock starts again, so 9 + 5 = 14 hours shows as 2 o'clock. The next card shows why this is a remainder.
optionExplain: 9 + 5 = 14 is the right sum, but a clock face stops at 12, so 14 o'clock is never shown.
Right: the hand passes 12 and goes on 2 more hours, since 14 is one turn of 12 plus 2.
This is one hour short, which happens if you count 9 itself as the first hour: 9, 10, 11, 12, 1.
5 is how many hours pass, not where the hand ends up; the count has to start from 9.

questions.explain: \(23 = 1 \times 12 + 11\), so the remainder is 11. On a clock, 23:00 shows as 11 o'clock.
questions.rule: Take away whole twelves; what is left, from 0 to 11, is the answer.

questions.q: It is 10 o'clock now. A train journey takes 27 hours. What does a 12-hour clock show when the train arrives?
questions.explain: The arrival is 10 + 27 = 37 hours on from 12. Since \(37 = 3 \times 12 + 1\), the clock shows 1 o'clock.
optionExplain: 3 is \(27 \bmod 12\), the remainder of the journey alone. It forgets to start counting from 10 o'clock.
10 + 3 = 13 adds the right remainder but forgets to wrap around a second time: 13 o'clock is 1 o'clock.
Right: \(10 + 27 = 37\) and \(37 = 3 \times 12 + 1\), so the hand points to 1.
27 hours feels like 'about a day', but only multiples of 12 bring the hand back; \(27 = 2 \times 12 + 3\).
questions.hint: Add the journey to the start time first, then remove whole twelves.
questions.rule: Add first, then wrap around as many times as needed.

questions.q: Select every number that leaves remainder 5 when divided by 12.
questions.explain: 17, 29, 41 and 53 are \(12 + 5\), \(2 \times 12 + 5\), \(3 \times 12 + 5\) and \(4 \times 12 + 5\). Each is 12 more than the one before, so they all point to 5 on the clock.
optionExplain: 15 ends in 5, which is tempting, but \(15 = 12 + 3\), so its remainder is 3.
Right: \(29 = 2 \times 12 + 5\).
Right: \(41 = 3 \times 12 + 5\), one more full turn than 29.
50 is close to 53, but \(50 = 4 \times 12 + 2\), so its remainder is 2.
Right: \(53 = 4 \times 12 + 5\).
questions.rule: Numbers with the same remainder mod 12 are 12 apart.
questions.teaches: The numbers with remainder 5 mod 12 form a list 5, 17, 29, 41, 53, ... in which each is 12 more than the last, because adding a full turn never moves the hand.

questions.q: Each question is answered by one part of a division with remainder. Sort them: is the answer the quotient (number of full rounds) or the remainder (what is left over)?

items.t: How many full turns the hour hand makes in 29 hours
Which number the hour hand points to after 29 hours
How many full boxes 50 eggs fill, 12 to a box
How many loose eggs remain after boxing 50 eggs, 12 to a box
How many complete weeks there are in 45 days
How many extra days there are beyond the complete weeks in 45 days

questions.explain: \(29 = 2 \times 12 + 5\), \(50 = 4 \times 12 + 2\) and \(45 = 6 \times 7 + 3\). The quotients 2, 4 and 6 count full rounds; the remainders 5, 2 and 3 say where you end up.
questions.rule: The quotient counts full rounds; the remainder says where you land.

questions.q: A kitchen timer's minute hand starts at 0 and runs for 175 minutes. Which minute mark does the minute hand point to at the end?
questions.explain: The minute hand goes round once every 60 minutes, so divide by 60: \(175 = 2 \times 60 + 55\). It points to minute 55.
optionExplain: Right: the cycle for minutes has length 60, and \(175 = 2 \times 60 + 55\).
\(175 \bmod 12 = 7\). Dividing by 12 is a habit from the hour hand, but the minute hand needs 60 minutes, not 12, to go round.
2 is the quotient: the number of full turns. It says how often the hand went round, not where it points.
175 minus 100 is 75, but a minute hand has no 75 mark; take away whole 60s until less than 60 is left.
questions.hint: How many minutes does the minute hand need to go all the way round?
questions.rule: Divide by the length of the cycle.
questions.teaches: The number you divide by (the modulus) is the length of the cycle, so the same method works for any cycle: 60 for minutes, 24 for a 24-hour clock, 12 for hours.

questions.q: On a 12-hour clock, the hour hand points to the same number 3 hours after midnight and 15 hours after midnight.
questions.explain: 15 hours is one full turn of 12 hours plus 3, and a full turn leaves the hand where it was. The next card gives this 'same position' a name.
questions.rule: Numbers that differ by a full turn land in the same place.

questions.q: Which statement means the same as \(38 \equiv 14 \pmod{12}\)?
options: 14 is the remainder of 38 divided by 12
38 and 14 leave the same remainder when divided by 12
questions.explain: Congruence means equal remainders. Here both are 2: \(38 = 3 \times 12 + 2\) and \(14 = 12 + 2\). Their difference 24 is a multiple of 12, as the second test needs.
optionExplain: The symbol looks a bit like a division sum, but \(38 \div 12\) is about 3.2, not 14.
The difference must be a multiple of 12, not 12 itself. Here 38 - 14 = 24, which is 2 x 12, and that is enough.
A remainder mod 12 is always below 12, so it cannot be 14; the remainder of 38 is 2.
Right: both leave remainder 2, which is exactly what \(\equiv\) says.

questions.explain: Use the difference test: is the difference a multiple of 12? 24, 36 and 48 are; 20, 30 and 10 are not.
optionExplain: False: \(26 - 6 = 20\), not a multiple of 12. Both numbers end in 6, which is tempting, but \(26 \bmod 12 = 2\).
False: both contain the digit 3, but \(33 - 3 = 30\) is not a multiple of 12; \(33 \bmod 12 = 9\).
False: both end in 9, but \(19 - 9 = 10\), which is not a multiple of 12; \(19 \bmod 12 = 7\).
questions.rule: Subtract and ask: is the difference a multiple of n? Matching last digits prove nothing mod 12.

questions.q: \(26 \equiv 2 \pmod{12}\) is true. The largest n for which \(26 \equiv 2 \pmod{n}\) is also true is ____.
questions.explain: \(26 \equiv 2 \pmod{n}\) holds exactly when n divides \(26 - 2 = 24\). So it holds for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24, and the largest is 24.
questions.hint: Work out 26 - 2 first. Which numbers divide it?
questions.rule: \(a \equiv b \pmod{n}\) holds for exactly the n that divide \(a - b\).
questions.teaches: One subtraction answers the question for every modulus at once: \(a \equiv b\) is true mod each divisor of \(a - b\) and false for every other n.

questions.q: Suppose you know that \(a \equiv b \pmod{12}\). Then \(a \equiv b \pmod{6}\) must also be true.
questions.explain: If \(a - b\) is a multiple of 12, it is also a multiple of 6, since 12 = 2 x 6. The reverse fails: \(8 \equiv 2 \pmod{6}\) but not mod 12, because 6 is not a multiple of 12.
questions.rule: Congruent mod n means congruent mod every divisor of n, but not the other way round.

questions.q: Match each congruence with the everyday description of the whole number x that means the same thing.
pairs: x ends in the digit 0 or 5
x eggs fill whole boxes of 12 exactly
questions.explain: Remainder 0 mod 2 means x splits into pairs: even. Remainder 1 mod 2 means one is left over: odd. The multiples of 5 are 5, 10, 15, 20, ..., which end in 5 or 0. Remainder 0 mod 12 means whole dozens with none left over.
questions.rule: 'Even', 'odd' and 'a multiple of' are all congruence statements.
questions.teaches: Ideas you already knew are congruences in disguise: even means \(x \equiv 0 \pmod 2\), odd means \(x \equiv 1 \pmod 2\), and 'a multiple of k' means \(x \equiv 0 \pmod k\).

questions.q: Sam checks whether \(52 \equiv 4 \pmod{12}\). Step 1: \(52 - 4 = 48\). Step 2: 48 is not 12, so 52 and 4 are not congruent mod 12. Which step is wrong?
options: Step 1: the difference must be 4 - 52, not 52 - 4
Step 2: 48 only has to be a multiple of 12, and 48 = 4 x 12
Neither step: 52 and 4 really are not congruent mod 12
Step 1: you must divide by 12 first and never subtract
questions.explain: The test asks whether \(a - b\) is a multiple of n, not whether it equals n. \(48 = 4 \times 12\), so \(52 \equiv 4 \pmod{12}\); indeed \(52 = 4 \times 12 + 4\).
optionExplain: Order does not matter: 4 - 52 = -48 is a multiple of 12 exactly when 48 is.
Right: 'n divides a - b' means a - b is some multiple of n. Four full turns is as good as one.
Tempting if you trust Step 2, but \(52 = 4 \times 12 + 4\) leaves remainder 4, the same as 4.
Both tests are valid; the difference test is often quicker. The mistake is in how Step 2 reads the result.
questions.rule: Multiple of n, not equal to n.
